outputs.L1:
On the ground can spook a horse who won’t flinch when faced with a backhoe or a pack of Harleys. I call it “horse ophthalmology” because it is a different kind of system—not necessarily celestial, but a vision in which the small, the wispy, the lightly lifted or stirring threads of existence excite more fear than louder, larger bodies do.

It’s Matthew who said that the light of the body is the eye, and that if the eye is healthy, the whole body will be full of light. Perhaps, in this case, “light” can also mean “lightness.” With my eyes of corrupted and corruptible flesh, I’m afraid I see mostly darkness—by which I mean heaviness. How great is that darkness? Not as great as the inner weightlessness of horses whose eyes perceive—correctly, I believe—the threat of annihilation in every windblown dust mote of malignant life.

All these years, I’ve been watching warily in the obvious places: in bars, in wars, in night cities and nightmares, on furious seas. Yet what has been trying to destroy me has lain hidden inside friendly-seeming breezes, behind soft music, beneath the carpet of small things one can barely see.

The eye is also a lamp, says Matthew—a giver of light, a bestower of incandescent honey, which I will pour more cautiously over the courses I travel from now on. What’s that whisper? Just the delicate sweeping away of somebody’s life.
outputs.L2:
Something underfoot may terrify a horse that remains perfectly calm before an excavator or a roaring group of Harley motorcycles. I think of this as “horseophthalmology”: a unique mode of perception, not necessarily heavenly, in which tiny, filmy, barely raised or trembling strands of life seem more dangerous than anything massive or noisy. Matthew writes that the eye provides the body’s light, and that a sound eye fills the entire body with illumination. Here, perhaps, “light” might signify not only brightness but also an absence of weight.

Through eyes made of flesh—already damaged and always capable of further corruption—I tend to perceive darkness, or rather, burden and density. How vast is that darkness? It is still less powerful than the inward buoyancy of horses, whose sight rightly detects, I believe, the possibility of extinction in each malignant speck of life carried by the wind.

For years I have kept a cautious watch on the places where danger seems obvious: taverns, battlefields, cities after dark, nightmares, and raging oceans. But the forces seeking my ruin have been concealed in apparently harmless currents of air, behind gentle melodies, and below a covering of nearly invisible details.

Matthew also describes the eye as a lamp: a source of radiance, dispensing luminous honey. From now on, I will spill that honey more carefully across the paths before me. What is that faint sound? Merely the soft brushing away of someone’s existence.
outputs.L3:
A horse may remain perfectly calm in the presence of large, noisy machines, yet suddenly become frightened by the smallest and most subtle movement. This peculiar sensitivity is what the speaker calls “horseophthalmology”: a distinctive way of seeing that detects danger in the lightest, quietest, and most easily overlooked things.

Drawing on Matthew’s teaching that the eye is the light of the body, the speaker connects this heightened perception to a spiritual understanding of vision. True sight is associated with lightness and illumination, while corrupted human vision becomes heavy, clouded, and dark. The problem is not simply that people fail to see obvious dangers; rather, their damaged perception prevents them from recognizing the faint signs through which danger often approaches.

The speaker gradually realizes that the most genuine threats have not appeared in places openly marked by violence or destruction. Instead, they have remained concealed within what seems ordinary, gentle, and nearly invisible. Like the slight movement that startles a horse more than the roar of machinery, these quiet details may contain warnings that human beings are too distracted or spiritually burdened to notice.

This realization changes the speaker’s way of moving through the world. Rather than looking only for dramatic or unmistakable signs of danger, the speaker proceeds more cautiously, attending to minor disturbances, delicate shifts, and barely perceptible signals. Such vigilance arises from the recognition that destruction and death may announce themselves not through spectacle, but through the faintest movements at the edge of vision.
outputs.L4:
Horses are not always frightened by what seems truly dangerous. They may stand calmly beside a roaring engine or carry a rider through noise and confusion, yet suddenly shy at a scrap of paper trembling in the grass, a pale ribbon caught on a fence, or a wisp of plastic lifted by the wind. What alarms them is often not the solid, recognizable object but the slight and uncertain movement at the edge of sight. Their fear gathers around what cannot be clearly identified.

I have often thought that human beings are not so different. We prepare ourselves for obvious dangers: open hostility, visible violence, unmistakable betrayal. Because such threats have names and shapes, we imagine that we will recognize them in time. Yet many of the forces that alter our lives arrive almost unnoticed. A hesitation in someone’s voice, a small change in habit, a glance quickly withdrawn, or a thought repeatedly dismissed as unimportant may contain more warning than a loud declaration. The smallest signs can reveal what larger appearances conceal.

Matthew’s image of the eye as the lamp of the body gives this idea a deeper meaning. If the eye is clear, the whole body is filled with light; if the eye is clouded, darkness spreads within. Seeing, in this sense, is not merely the physical act of looking. It is a form of attention and judgment. What we notice—and what we choose not to notice—shapes our understanding of the world. A careless gaze can leave us exposed even when our eyes are open.

The most serious dangers do not always announce themselves with noise. They may hide in familiar places or approach in forms too slight to awaken suspicion. Like the horse startled by a wavering strand in the wind, we sense that uncertainty itself can be a warning. But unlike the horse, we often train ourselves to ignore such impressions, dismissing them as irrational because they do not yet amount to proof.

This does not mean that every shadow should become a source of fear. It means that attention must be finer than simple watchfulness. We must learn to distinguish between empty alarm and the quiet detail that reveals a larger truth. Life asks us to look carefully, especially at what appears insignificant. The danger may not be the charging figure in the open field. It may be the nearly invisible movement at its edge, waiting for the light to shift before it can be seen.
outputs.L5:
Harleys thundered along the empty highway, their engines breaking the desert silence. At the front rode a stranger everyone called **Matthewwho**, a name earned because no one knew where he came from—or whether Matthew was even his real name.

Their destination was a fading town called **Maybein**, a place found on old maps but missing from new ones. Some said it had been abandoned years ago. Others claimed it appeared only to travelers who had nowhere else to go.

As the sun sank behind the hills, the riders saw a flickering sign ahead:

**MAYBEIN — POPULATION: MAYBE**

Matthewwho slowed his Harley and smiled. “This is the place.”

No one asked how he knew. They simply followed him into town, while the road quietly disappeared behind them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose meditation about why horses fear tiny, windblown objects but remain calm around loud machinery, connecting their vision to Matthew’s saying that “the eye is the lamp of the body.”
counterfactuals.output:
A horse may stand quietly beside a tractor coughing iron thunder into the morning, yet shy from a grocery bag skittering across the road. This is not foolishness. The machine declares itself: immense, noisy, steady in its purpose. Its sound has a source; its movement follows a path. But the little white bag is a scrap of uncertainty. It lifts without warning, collapses, darts sideways, becomes bird, fang, flame. To an animal shaped by flight, what cannot be predicted may be more alarming than what is merely loud.

A horse’s eyes are set wide, gathering the world from nearly every side. Such vision is a mercy for prey: danger may be seen before it arrives. Yet every mercy carries its burden. The edges of the world are always entering the horse’s awareness—shadows, flutterings, sudden changes of shape. The horse sees broadly, but not always with the settled clarity by which the mind says, *This is harmless.* Often the body answers first.

“The eye is the lamp of the body,” says Matthew. Perhaps this means not only that sight admits the world, but that the manner of our seeing illuminates—or darkens—everything within us. What the eye receives, the heart must interpret. A familiar engine may enter as noise and become nothing; a leaf twisting in the wind may enter as a threat and flood the whole body with night.

We are not so different. We endure the great machinery of our days—the traffic, the deadlines, the public storms—because we have learned their rhythms. Yet some small thing, a glance, a rumor, an unanswered message, blows across the corner of our vision and startles us into fear. The soul, too, is a grazing animal. It longs for open ground and watches the margins.

Perhaps wisdom is not to despise the startled horse, in ourselves or in another, but to lead it gently toward the trembling thing. Let the eye look again. Let the lamp be cleared of panic. Let what seemed a predator become only paper, only leaf, only wind borrowing a shape for a moment.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, poetic paragraph in the style of a contemporary nature essayist. Coin the term “horseophthalmology” and explore lightness, darkness, fear, mortality, and the hidden dangers in ordinary things.
counterfactuals.output: I have begun to think of horseophthalmology as the study not of the horse’s eye, but of everything the horse sees and will not tell us: the white gate floating at dusk, the black bag snagged on a fence and breathing like a lung, the harmless puddle holding a second sky deep enough to drown in. A horse knows that lightness is never innocent; a leaf can lift like a startled hand, a feather can flash with the pallor of bone, and sunlight itself may sharpen on a window into a blade. Darkness, meanwhile, is not empty but crowded—fox, ditch, wire, the old machinery of fear turning beneath the grass. We call these things ordinary because they have not yet killed us. The bucket waits with its bright handle, the apple conceals its seeds, the road lies down obediently before gathering speed. Mortality enters quietly, wearing the shapes we trust: a latch, a hoofprint filling with rain, a length of blue twine trembling in the hedge. Perhaps this is what the horse’s wide eye teaches—that survival depends on suspecting the beautiful, that terror is sometimes a form of attention, and that every field, however mild in morning light, keeps one dark corner folded under its tongue.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Continue this fragment as literary nonfiction: “A scrap of plastic on the ground can spook a horse who won’t flinch when faced with a backhoe or a pack of Harleys.” Include biblical imagery and end with an ominous whisper.
counterfactuals.output:
“A scrap of plastic on the ground can spook a horse who won’t flinch when faced with a backhoe or a pack of Harleys.”

Fear has never been reasonable, in horses or in us. It comes sidelong, a pale flicker at the edge of the known world. The mare will stand while diesel engines hammer the earth and chrome machines roar past like beasts from Revelation, yet a grocery bag snagged on sagebrush becomes a white-winged omen. Her nostrils widen. Every muscle gathers beneath the saddle. For one suspended second, she is no longer domesticated but ancient—an animal listening for the lion beyond the firelight.

You can feel her question travel up through the reins: *Do you see it? Do you understand what it is?*

Often, I don’t. I only know that the smallest things carry the longest shadows. A letter folded twice. A missed call after midnight. A spot on an X-ray no larger than a mustard seed. We boast of the catastrophes we have endured—the wrecks, the funerals, the years when the bank account ran dry—but tremble before some harmless scrap skittering across an ordinary afternoon.

In scripture, God arrives in flame, flood, whirlwind. But terror prefers humbler disguises. It waits in the rustle under the juniper, in the serpent’s narrow track through dust, in the silence after the cock crows. It knows that the gate to panic is seldom grand. It is a hairline opening, almost invisible, through which the whole dark wilderness may enter.

I speak to the mare until her breathing slows. I let her look. The plastic lifts and settles, lifts and settles, making its little counterfeit resurrection. At last she steps forward, trembling but obedient, and passes it by.

Behind us, the wind rises.

The bag tears free.

And something in the dry grass whispers, *Not yet.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental prose poem about equine perception, suggesting that horses correctly recognize the threat of annihilation in dust motes and gentle breezes while humans look for danger only in obvious places such as wars, bars, storms, and nightmares.
counterfactuals.output:
**FIELD OF VISION**

The horse startles at what we call nothing—

a mote unfastening itself from the rafters,  
a small gold planet crossing the barn’s dark;  
the mild hand of wind turning one blade of grass  
against the agreement of the field.

We laugh, palm the warm geography of the neck.  
Easy, we say, though the horse has already seen  
the white door inside the particle,  
the whole world powdered there: bone, fence, moon,  
our names rubbed clean from the buckets.

A breeze arrives without weapons.  
Still, the herd lifts its many-headed listening.  
Every flank becomes a question.  
Every eye, black and lateral, reads the fine print  
where extinction enters softly,

not with trumpets but with thistle-down,  
not with fire but the shift of a shadow  
from one hoof to another.

We prefer our dangers legible:  
wars with their bright mouths,  
bars with their bottles and broken teeth,  
storms dragging iron furniture through the sky,  
nightmares that sign their work in sweat.

We build a small museum of obvious endings  
and call ourselves vigilant.

But the horse knows annihilation is shy.  
It practices in dust.  
It rehearses beneath the loose sleeve of air.  
It can hide in the almost-sound behind the sound,  
in the grass bowing when no body passes.

Look: the horse has become still enough  
to outrun us.

Its ears turn toward the invisible.  
Its nostrils widen around the future.

And we, standing beside it,  
see only a peaceful field,  
only evening coming gently,  
gently—

as if gentleness  
had never erased a world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a philosophical monologue in which a narrator reflects on watching horses, quotes the Gospel of Matthew about the healthy eye and light, plays on the double meaning of “light,” and concludes that seemingly delicate things may conceal death.
counterfactuals.output:
I have watched horses for hours, watched them lower their dark heads to the grass as if listening for a word buried beneath the earth. Their gentleness is persuasive. The long lashes, the tremor of skin beneath a fly, the breath drifting pale from the nostrils—everything about them seems to belong to a quieter world.

And yet there is weight in them: bone, muscle, the sudden thunder of flight. What appears tender may, in an instant, become immense.

“The light of the body is the eye,” says the Gospel of Matthew. “If therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.” I have often wondered what it means for an eye to be healthy: not merely to see clearly, but to see without dividing the world into what comforts us and what frightens us. Perhaps such an eye makes the body light—bright with understanding, yes, but also unburdened, freed from the heaviness of illusion.

Still, light itself can deceive. We call a feather light because it scarcely weighs upon the hand; we call dawn light because it reveals the hand that holds it. Yet illumination does not make a thing harmless, and delicacy is not innocence. The sun glitters on a blade. A flower may carry poison. A horse’s fine ankle bears the force of a falling world.

So I watch them move through the field, beautiful as thoughts one is afraid to finish. Their grace does not abolish danger; it veils it. Perhaps that is what the healthy eye must learn at last: to look steadily upon fragile shapes and see, without hatred or surprise, the death they may conceal.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
